steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a paper proposing CosSIF, a cosine-similarity-based image filtering algorithm used before or after GAN training to deal with low inter-class variation and class imbalance in synthetic medical image datasets.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. Deep learning in medical image analysis
2. Challenge: limited, imbalanced data with low inter-class variation
3. GANs for class imbalance and their problem with low inter-class variation
4. Our proposal: CosSIF, FBGT and FAGT
5. Contributions
6. Paper organization

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. Deep learning in medical image analysis
- medical image analysis: diagnosis, treatment, monitoring of diseases
- deep learning: big improvements in early detection and classification
- many studies show efficacy; adopted in radiology, dermatology, ophthalmology
- radiology: beat radiologists for breast cancer in mammography
- dermatology: skin cancer from dermoscopy images
- ophthalmology: diabetic retinopathy, age-related macular degeneration from retinal images

2. Data challenge
- limited datasets; esp. classification: hard to get balanced data with high inter-class variation
- inter-class variation = appearance differences between classes
- imbalance when some classes are hard to collect
- Zech et al.: pneumonia in chest radiographs, model hurt by imbalance; low prevalence of pneumonia -> few positives
- low inter-class variation + imbalance undermine deep learning in medical imaging

3. GANs
- increasingly popular for class imbalance
- generate synthetic images resembling real ones
- success in many domains incl. medical image analysis
- conventional: train GAN on every minority-class image
- problem with low inter-class variation: synthetic images look like other classes -> technically balanced but hard to separate
- cause: lack of diversity in synthetic images -> no discriminative features

4. CosSIF
- Cosine Similarity-based Image Filtering; two methods FBGT (Filtering Before GAN Training), FAGT (Filtering After GAN Training)
- similarity between two sets of images: e.g. classes A and B, each A image vs all B images
- scores used by FBGT/FAGT to filter out most similar or dissimilar images
- FBGT: remove real minority images resembling other classes before GAN training; requires retraining GAN
- FAGT: on pre-trained GAN, compare synthetic images to real training images
- architecture in Fig. 1
- evaluation: ViT, Swin Transformer, ConvNeXt

5. Contributions
- CosSIF, cosine similarity backbone, finds images of one class similar to other class(es)
- FBGT and FAGT to regulate GAN synthetic generation
- reproducible train-test split for HAM10000
- ISIC-2016: FAGT beats MelaNet in sensitivity by 1.59% and AUC by 1.88%; FBGT beats IRv2+SA in recall by 13.75%; FAGT alone max accuracy 94.44%

6. Organization
- Sec 2: related work on class imbalance, low inter-class variation; cosine similarity in computer vision
- next: CosSIF, FBGT, FAGT, GAN architecture, transformer and convolutional models
- Sec 4: datasets, classifier and GAN training configs, experiments
- Sec 5: ablation study, comparison with baselines
- Sec 6: conclusions, future work

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Medical image analysis is a very important part of modern healthcare, since it enables accurate diagnosis, effective treatment, and continuous monitoring of various diseases. Deep learning has opened a new horizon in this field and has given significant improvements in the early detection and classification of diseases. Many studies have shown that deep learning is effective in medical imaging, and so it has been widely adopted in multiple medical domains, including radiology, dermatology, and ophthalmology. In radiology, deep learning models have been more accurate than radiologists at detecting breast cancer in mammography images. In dermatology, deep learning has also shown outstanding performance in identifying skin cancer from dermoscopy images. And in ophthalmology, deep learning models have been used to diagnose diabetic retinopathy and age-related macular degeneration from retinal images.

A major challenge in developing deep learning models for medical image analysis is that there are not many datasets available. This is a big issue in classification tasks, where it is hard to get a balanced dataset with high inter-class variation. Inter-class variation means the differences in appearance between different classes of images. The lack of balanced datasets happens when it is hard to get enough images from some classes, so the classes end up with an imbalanced distribution. For example, Zech et al. reported that training a deep learning model to detect pneumonia in chest radiographs was significantly affected by the imbalanced dataset. They noted that it was difficult to get a balanced dataset with enough images of the positive class because pneumonia has a low prevalence in the population. So low inter-class variation and class imbalance in medical image datasets really undermine how applicable deep learning techniques are in medical imaging.

Generative adversarial networks (GANs) have become more and more popular in recent years for addressing class imbalance in datasets. GANs are generative models that can produce synthetic images which closely resemble real images. Several studies have reported success with GANs for class imbalance in various domains, including medical image analysis. The usual way to train a GAN is to use every image of the minority class in a dataset. But this can be a problem when the images have low inter-class variation. The GAN may generate synthetic images that look like images from other classes, so the dataset is technically balanced but a neural network has a hard time distinguishing the differences between classes. This is mostly because of the lack of diversity in the synthetic images, which makes it hard for a network to learn the discriminative features that are needed for accurate classification.

[CosSIF proposal]
- CosSIF; FBGT and FAGT
- similarity of each class-A image vs all class-B images; scores used to filter most similar or dissimilar
- FBGT: remove minority real images resembling other classes before GAN training; needs GAN retraining
- FAGT: pre-trained GAN, synthetic vs real training images
- Fig. 1 architecture; experiments with ViT, Swin Transformer, ConvNeXt

[Contributions]
- CosSIF algorithm with cosine similarity backbone
- FBGT and FAGT to regulate GAN generation
- reproducible HAM10000 train-test split
- ISIC-2016: FAGT vs MelaNet sensitivity +1.59%, AUC +1.88%; FBGT vs IRv2+SA recall +13.75%; FAGT alone max accuracy 94.44%

[Organization]
- Sec 2 related work + cosine similarity in CV; then methods + GAN + classifiers; Sec 4 datasets, configs, experiments; Sec 5 ablation + baselines; Sec 6 conclusions, future work

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Medical image analysis is a very important part of modern healthcare, since it enables accurate diagnosis, effective treatment, and continuous monitoring of various diseases. Deep learning has opened a new horizon in this field and has given significant improvements in the early detection and classification of diseases. Many studies have shown that deep learning is effective in medical imaging, and so it has been widely adopted in multiple medical domains, including radiology, dermatology, and ophthalmology. In radiology, deep learning models have been more accurate than radiologists at detecting breast cancer in mammography images. In dermatology, deep learning has also shown outstanding performance in identifying skin cancer from dermoscopy images. And in ophthalmology, deep learning models have been used to diagnose diabetic retinopathy and age-related macular degeneration from retinal images.

A major challenge in developing deep learning models for medical image analysis is that there are not many datasets available. This is a big issue in classification tasks, where it is hard to get a balanced dataset with high inter-class variation. Inter-class variation means the differences in appearance between different classes of images. The lack of balanced datasets happens when it is hard to get enough images from some classes, so the classes end up with an imbalanced distribution. For example, Zech et al. reported that training a deep learning model to detect pneumonia in chest radiographs was significantly affected by the imbalanced dataset. They noted that it was difficult to get a balanced dataset with enough images of the positive class because pneumonia has a low prevalence in the population. So low inter-class variation and class imbalance in medical image datasets really undermine how applicable deep learning techniques are in medical imaging.

Generative adversarial networks (GANs) have become more and more popular in recent years for addressing class imbalance in datasets. GANs are generative models that can produce synthetic images which closely resemble real images. Several studies have reported success with GANs for class imbalance in various domains, including medical image analysis. The usual way to train a GAN is to use every image of the minority class in a dataset. But this can be a problem when the images have low inter-class variation. The GAN may generate synthetic images that look like images from other classes, so the dataset is technically balanced but a neural network has a hard time distinguishing the differences between classes. This is mostly because of the lack of diversity in the synthetic images, which makes it hard for a network to learn the discriminative features that are needed for accurate classification.

To deal with the challenge of GANs producing visually similar images with less discriminative features when they are trained on datasets with low inter-class variation, we propose a new filtering algorithm called Cosine Similarity-based Image Filtering (CosSIF). We use CosSIF to introduce two filtering methods, Filtering Before GAN Training (FBGT) and Filtering After GAN Training (FAGT). CosSIF is used to determine the similarity between two sets of images. For example, if a dataset has two classes A and B, CosSIF calculates the similarity of each image from class A with all the images in class B. The similarity scores from CosSIF are then used by FBGT or FAGT to filter out the most similar or dissimilar images. FBGT removes real images from the minority class that look like images from other classes, before they are put into the training dataset of a GAN. This makes sure the GAN does not learn certain features that lead to generating visually similar images. But FBGT requires retraining the GAN with the filtered images. FAGT, on the other hand, works on a pre-trained GAN, and the similarity calculations are done between the synthetic images generated by the GAN and the real images that were used to train the GAN. Fig. 1 shows the architecture of our proposed algorithm and filtering methods. To evaluate how effective our approaches are, we run experiments with modern transformers like Vision Transformer (ViT) and Swin Transformer, and also convolutional-based networks like ConvNeXt. The key contributions of this paper are:

- We propose CosSIF, an image similarity calculation algorithm that has cosine similarity as its backbone and can identify images of a specific class that are visually similar to images of another class/classes in a dataset.

- We propose two filtering methods, FBGT and FAGT, to regulate the synthetic image generation of GANs in order to reduce low inter-class variability in medical image datasets.

- We propose a reproducible train-test split for the HAM10000 dataset, so that our methods can be compared with future experiments by others.

- We show experimentally that using FAGT on the ISIC-2016 dataset beats the baseline method, MelaNet, in sensitivity by 1.59% and in AUC by 1.88%. Also, using FBGT beats the baseline method IRv2+SA in recall by 13.75%, and using only FAGT reaches a maximum accuracy of 94.44%.

The rest of this paper is organized as follows. In Section 2 we discuss related studies on class imbalance and low inter-class variation in medical image classification, and we also look at how cosine similarity is used in computer vision. Then we give an overview of our proposed CosSIF algorithm and the FBGT and FAGT filtering methods, and this section also describes our selected GAN architecture and gives a short overview of the transformer and convolutional-based network models we chose. In Section 4 we give an overview of the datasets used and present the configurations for classifier and GAN training, and then we do experiments with our proposed algorithm and filtering methods. In Section 5 we do an ablation study of our experiments and compare our trained classifiers against baseline methods. Finally, Section 6 gives the conclusions and discusses possible future work.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Medical image analysis is a critical component of modern healthcare, enabling accurate diagnosis, effective treatment, and continuous monitoring of various diseases [1]. The advent of deep learning has opened a new horizon in this field, delivering significant improvements in the early detection and classification of diseases. Numerous studies have highlighted the efficacy of deep learning in medical imaging [2,3], leading to its widespread adoption in multiple medical domains, including radiology, dermatology, and ophthalmology [4,5,6]. In radiology, deep learning models have surpassed the diagnostic accuracy of radiologists in detecting breast cancer in mammography images [7]. Similarly, in dermatology, deep learning has shown outstanding performance in identifying skin cancer from dermoscopy images [8]. In ophthalmology, deep learning models have been used to diagnose diabetic retinopathy and age-related macular degeneration from retinal images [9,10].

One of the major challenges in developing deep learning models for medical image analysis is the limited availability of datasets. This issue is particularly significant in classification tasks, where obtaining a balanced dataset with high inter-class variation is difficult [11]. Inter-class variation refers to the differences in appearance between different classes of images [12]. The scarcity of balanced datasets arises when it is hard to obtain a sufficient number of images from certain classes, resulting in an imbalanced distribution of classes. For example, Zech et al. [13] reported that training a deep learning model to detect pneumonia in chest radiographs was significantly impacted by the imbalanced nature of the dataset. The authors noted that obtaining a balanced dataset with enough images of the positive class was difficult due to the low prevalence of pneumonia in the population. Low inter-class variation and class imbalance in medical image datasets therefore significantly undermine the applicability of deep learning techniques in medical imaging.

The use of generative adversarial networks (GANs) to address class imbalance in datasets has gained popularity in recent years [14]. GANs are generative models that can produce synthetic images closely resembling real images [15]. Several studies have reported success using GANs to address class imbalance in various domains, including medical image analysis [16]. The conventional approach to training a GAN uses every image of the minority class in a dataset [17]. However, this method can be problematic when dealing with images that have low inter-class variation, because the GAN may generate synthetic images that visually resemble images from other classes. The result is a dataset that is technically balanced but makes it hard for a neural network to distinguish differences between classes. This is largely attributed to the lack of diversity in the synthetic images, which makes it difficult for a network to learn the discriminative features required for accurate classification.

In response to the challenge of GANs producing visually similar images with less discriminative features when trained on datasets with low inter-class variation, we propose a novel filtering algorithm called Cosine Similarity-based Image Filtering (CosSIF). We use CosSIF to introduce two filtering methods: Filtering Before GAN Training (FBGT) and Filtering After GAN Training (FAGT). The CosSIF algorithm determines the similarity between two sets of images. For instance, in a dataset consisting of two classes, A and B, CosSIF calculates the similarity of each image from class A with all the images in class B. The resulting similarity scores are then used by FBGT or FAGT to filter out the most similar or dissimilar images. FBGT removes real images from the minority class that visually resemble images from other classes before they are incorporated into the training dataset of a GAN. This ensures that the GAN does not learn certain features that contribute to generating visually similar images. However, FBGT requires retraining the GAN with the filtered images. In contrast, FAGT operates on a pre-trained GAN, with similarity calculations conducted between the synthetic images generated by the GAN and the real images used to train it. The architecture of our proposed algorithm and filtering methods is illustrated in Fig. 1. To evaluate the effectiveness of our approaches, we perform experiments using modern transformers such as Vision Transformer (ViT) and Swin Transformer, as well as convolutional-based networks like ConvNeXt. The key contributions of this paper can be summarized as follows:

- We propose CosSIF, an image similarity calculation algorithm with cosine similarity as its backbone, capable of identifying images of a specific class that are visually similar to images of another class/classes in a dataset.

- We propose two filtering methods, FBGT and FAGT, to regulate the synthetic image generation capabilities of GANs in an effort to reduce low inter-class variability in medical image datasets.

- We propose a reproducible train-test split for the HAM10000 dataset, which can facilitate the comparison of our proposed methods with future experiments by others.

- We experimentally demonstrate that using FAGT on the ISIC-2016 dataset surpasses the baseline method, MelaNet [18], in sensitivity by 1.59% and in AUC by 1.88%. Furthermore, using FBGT exceeds the baseline method, IRv2+SA [19], in recall by 13.75%, and the sole use of FAGT achieves a maximum accuracy of 94.44%.

The remaining sections of this paper are organized as follows. In Section 2, we discuss related studies on class imbalance and low inter-class variation in medical image classification and explore the usage of cosine similarity in computer vision. In Section 2, we present a comprehensive overview of our proposed CosSIF algorithm and of the FBGT and FAGT filtering methods; this section also describes our selected GAN architecture and briefly reviews our chosen transformer and convolutional-based network models. In Section 4, we give an overview of the datasets used and present the selected configurations for classifier and GAN training, and then perform experiments with our proposed algorithm and filtering methods. In Section 5, we conduct an ablation study of our experiments and compare the performance of our trained classifiers against baseline methods. Finally, Section 6 presents the conclusions and discusses possibilities for future work.
